transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I guess the main thing that finally pushed me to make this appointment—and honestly, my wife has been on my case about it for months, maybe years, but definitely more lately since I got promoted to manager—is that I just can't seem to hold my focus on anything for more than a few minutes. I mean, I'm a construction manager, right? So my days are packed. I'll sit down to lead a safety briefing with the guys, or I'll be staring at a set of blueprints for a plan review, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, you really need to pay attention to this, this is important, safety is number one." And I try, I really do try hard to lock in. But I swear, within two, maybe three minutes tops, my brain is just gone. 

It's like someone flips a switch and suddenly I'm thinking about the concrete pour scheduled for next Tuesday, or why the drywall guys are running two days behind on the second floor, or if I remembered to order the right gauge wire for the electricians. It's just three or four different job problems all hitting me at once. And while my mind is off running a marathon in five different directions, the briefing is still happening, or I'm still supposed to be reviewing the plans. Then, later on, I realize I completely missed things—things I absolutely know I should have caught if I had just been able to stay present. It's embarrassing, honestly. I've got 20 years in this business, I started from the bottom swinging a hammer, and I know this stuff inside and out, but if I can't even get through a basic safety meeting without checking out... I don't know, it's just getting really bad and it's starting to affect the job site.
Are you having trouble focusing or getting distracted at home or in your personal life as well?

At home? Man, yeah, it's... honestly, it might even be worse at home. Or maybe it just feels worse because it's my wife who has to deal with it, you know? Like, just last weekend, she asked me to fix the hinge on the back gate. Simple job, right? Five minutes, tops. I go out to the garage to get my drill, and while I'm looking for the right bit, I notice the workbench is a mess. So I start clearing off the workbench, but then I find this old box of fishing lures I thought I lost last summer. So I'm looking through the lures, thinking about maybe taking the boat out, and then I realize the boat battery probably needs charging. So I go to check the battery, and on the way, I see the dog's water bowl is empty. 

Two hours later, my wife comes out to the garage, and I'm halfway through reorganizing the entire shelving unit, the drill is sitting on the floor, and the gate is still broken. And she just looks at me with this... this face. It's not even angry anymore, it's just exhausted. And I try to explain, like, "Hey, I was getting to it, I just saw this other thing," but I know how it sounds. It sounds like an excuse. But I really didn't mean to blow off the gate! My brain just... it just grabbed onto the next thing, and the next thing, and the gate completely evaporated from my mind. 

And it's not just chores. It's conversations, too. We'll be sitting on the couch, watching a show, and she'll be telling me about her day at the bank—she's a loan officer, deals with a lot of stressful stuff—and I am looking right at her. I am nodding. But my brain is suddenly obsessing over whether I remembered to lock the truck, or why the dog is licking his paw, or this weird noise the refrigerator is making. And then she'll stop and say, "Are you even listening to me?" And I have to admit that I haven't heard a single word she said for the last five minutes. It makes her feel like I don't care, but I do! I really do. I just can't keep my head in the room. It's like I'm physically there, but mentally I'm just bouncing off the walls.
Do you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh, man, all the time. It’s actually a huge problem for me, especially at work. Like, I’ll be in a meeting with the subcontractors—say, the plumbing foreman and the HVAC guy—and they’ll start bringing up an issue with the ductwork overlapping the pipes. And they’ll barely get five words out, they’ll start saying, "Hey, on the third floor, the main line is—" and I just jump right in. I cut them off completely because my brain instantly connects the dots, or at least I *think* it does. I’m like, "Yeah, yeah, the clearance is too tight, just drop the ceiling frame an inch, we’ve got the room." 

I just blurt it out because I feel like I already know exactly where they’re going with the question, and my brain is moving so fast I just want to get the answer out and move on to the next fire I have to put out. But the thing is, half the time, I answer way too fast and then I realize I completely missed the actual point. Like, the plumber will just look at me and say, "Uh, no, the clearance is fine, the problem is the structural beam is in the way of the drop." And then I look like an idiot. Because I didn't let them finish the sentence, I missed the most important part of what they were trying to tell me. 

And it happens with my wife, too. She'll be trying to ask me something about our weekend plans, like, "Hey, for the barbecue on Sunday, did you want to—" and I’ll just yell out, "Burgers!" And she’ll just sigh and say, "I was going to ask if you wanted to invite your brother." It’s like I literally cannot wait for the end of the sentence. The words just fall out of my mouth before the other person has even finished taking a breath. It’s incredibly frustrating, and I know it pisses people off because it makes it seem like I think I’m the smartest guy in the room or that I don't care what they have to say, but I just... I can't seem to put the brakes on my own mouth.
Do you often act on impulses without thinking them through, like doing something sudden without considering the consequences?

Impulses? Like... like just doing something crazy out of nowhere? No, I... I don't really think so. I mean, not physically, anyway. You gotta understand, doc, in my line of work, if you just do something sudden without thinking, somebody gets killed. Literally. I've been on sites where, you know, a guy didn't think and just unhooked his fall harness to reach a tool, or decided to swing a boom lift around without checking his blind spot, and man, it's an absolute disaster. So I'm actually really, really strict about that kind of stuff. Safety first, always. I might run my mouth too fast, like I was just telling you about cutting off the plumbing foreman, but when it comes to actually *doing* things, taking actions... I don't just jump off a cliff without looking. 

Well, I mean... my wife might tell you that buying that Traeger smoker last summer was sudden. But the thing is, I had been thinking about getting a smoker for months! I just, you know, I didn't happen to mention it to her. So to her, it looked like I just walked into Home Depot for a box of drywall screws and walked out with an eight-hundred-dollar grill, but I had actually been researching the pellet feeds and the Wi-Fi temperature controls on my phone during my lunch breaks for a long time. So that doesn't really count as an impulse, right? Because I thought about it. I just didn't communicate it. 

But as far as just... acting recklessly, or doing stuff where I don't consider the consequences? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. You just can't survive twenty years in the trades if you're doing wild, unpredictable stuff. You have to respect what happens next. Like, I remember years ago when I was still a foreman framing out this commercial build, and one of the new kids just fired a nail gun without checking the backing. Missed my hand by maybe an inch. I chewed him out for a solid hour because you *have* to think about the consequences before you pull the trigger on something. So, yeah, no, I don't do things like that. My brain might bounce around a million miles an hour, but my feet stay on the ground, if that makes sense. I definitely don't just do things without thinking about what's gonna happen.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or having trouble sitting still?

Sitting still? Oh, man, sitting still is absolute torture for me. It really is. Like, you know those big OAC meetings we have to do? The Owner-Architect-Contractor sit-downs? We usually have them in these cramped little job site trailers, smelling like cheap coffee and drywall dust, and they can drag on for two, sometimes three hours. And I look around that folding table, and everybody else—the architects, the money guys, the engineers—they can just sit through the whole thing. They just plant themselves in those cheap plastic chairs and don't move a muscle for ninety minutes. I honestly do not understand how they do it. 

Because me? I'm the guy who is constantly up and down. I might last ten, maybe fifteen minutes in the chair before my legs just start feeling like they're plugged into a wall socket. Like I just have this overwhelming physical need to move. So I’m always the guy standing up. I'll push my chair back and walk over to the coffee pot and pour myself a cup of that awful black tar that I don't even want to drink, just so I have a reason to walk across the room. Or I'll stand at the back of the trailer and just lean against the wall, shifting my weight from one foot to the other, pacing a little bit. 

And if that's not enough, I'll start making excuses to actually leave the room entirely. I'll pat my pockets and pretend I left a pen in the truck, or I'll look at my phone—even if it didn't buzz—and go, "Oh, hold on, I gotta step outside to check on this lumber delivery real quick." Or I'll walk over to the big architectural prints taped to the wall and just stare at them, pretending I'm double-checking a window elevation, when really I just needed an excuse to move around. I always tell the suit-and-tie guys it's because I've got a bad lower back from my framing days, which, I mean, is true, my back isn't great, but that's not the real reason. The real reason is that if I have to sit still in a chair for more than twenty minutes, I feel like my skin is going to crawl right off my body. I just have to be in motion, you know? I have to be doing something.
Do you have mood swings or find yourself getting easily irritated?

Mood swings? Irritated? Nah, I wouldn't really say that. I mean... you'd think I would be, right? Given what I do for a living. Being a construction manager, you're basically a professional babysitter for grown men who play with heavy machinery, and there is always—and I mean *always*—something going wrong. 

But as far as my actual mood goes? It's pretty steady. I don't really get those up-and-down swings or find myself snapping at people over nothing. Like, I'll give you a perfect example. Just last Thursday, we had a 6 AM pour scheduled for this massive retaining wall on a new commercial lot. We had four trucks lined up out on the street, pump truck is primed and ready to go, the rebar is all tied off, and the first truck backs up to the hopper. And the concrete comes down the chute, and it is absolute soup. The slump was way off. Somebody at the plant messed up the mix, added way too much water, and if we poured that into the forms, the whole wall would fail inspection in a week. 

Now, the site super, this older guy named Gary, he completely lost his mind. He's throwing his hard hat, screaming at the driver—who's just a kid, it's not even his fault—and Gary is just totally red in the face, veins popping out of his neck, having a complete meltdown. But me? I didn't even get irritated. I just looked at it, grabbed my phone, and called the dispatcher to reject the load and get them to batch a new one. I didn't yell, I didn't get mad. I just shifted gears. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, if a guy does something genuinely unsafe, I'll chew him out, like I told you about that kid with the nail gun earlier. But that's not a mood swing, you know? That's just doing my job and making sure nobody goes to the hospital. But just getting irritated because the drywallers left their trash everywhere, or because the drive-thru messed up my coffee order, or just waking up in a bad mood for no reason? No, I don't really get that. I'm pretty much the same guy every day. I'm always moving a million miles an hour, yeah, and my brain is always jumping to the next problem, but I'm not angry or moody while I'm doing it. My wife actually tells me I'm annoyingly optimistic sometimes, even when everything on a site is falling apart and we're two weeks behind schedule. I just kind of roll with the punches. So yeah, I definitely wouldn't say I have mood swings or get easily irritated.
Do you have trouble organizing tasks or managing your time effectively?

Organizing? Yeah... yeah, that's, uh... that's a rough one for me, doc. Honestly, it's probably the biggest headache I deal with. If you want to know how I organize things, all you have to do is look at the cab of my truck. My truck is an absolute disaster area. I'm talking crumpled up invoices, empty Gatorade bottles, three different tape measures that I couldn't find so I kept buying new ones, and blueprints just shoved behind the seats. And my desk in the job trailer isn't any better. It's just piles. Piles of change orders, coffee cups, sticky notes that I wrote to myself three weeks ago and completely forgot about. 

Even my phone is a mess. You open the notes app on my phone, and it’s just a total disaster. I’ll have a note that just says something like "14 and 5/8ths" with absolutely no context. Is that a window opening? A pipe cut? I have no idea! Or I'll have a note that says "Call Gary" right above a grocery list, and I don't even remember which Gary I'm supposed to be calling. 

And the time management part... see, the problem is how things stack up on a site. It's never just one thing going wrong. It's always a pile-up. Like, on any given Tuesday, I’ll have RFIs—Requests for Information—that I need to write up and send back to the architects, and at the exact same time, the city inspector is pulling up for a rough-in inspection, the front office is hammering me for the monthly budget stuff, and my framing crew is having some massive drama because two guys didn't show up and they're behind. It all just hits at once. They're all stacked up right in front of me. 

And when that happens, I just... I freeze up in my head, because I honestly don’t know what to hit first. Everything feels like a massive emergency. So instead of just picking one thing and finishing it, I try to do it all, and I just jump around. I'll sit down at my messy desk, start typing an email for the RFI, get two sentences in, and then I'll hear the inspector outside, so I leave the email open and run out to walk the site with him. But while we're walking, I see the framing crew, so I ditch the inspector for a second to try and solve their manpower problem, and then my phone rings and it's the money guys asking about the budget. I just bounce from fire to fire to fire. And the result is that at the end of the day, I’ve touched ten different things, but I haven't actually completed a single one of them. Because I jump around so much, everything—and I mean everything—just runs late. I'm always apologizing for being behind schedule, always promising I'll get that paperwork in tomorrow. It's exhausting, honestly.
Have you experienced significant difficulties with inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity since childhood?

Childhood? Oh, man... yeah. Yeah, it’s not a new thing, doc. Not by a long shot. If you asked my mom, she’d probably talk your ear off about it for three days straight. I mean, going all the way back to elementary school, it was just... it was always a whole ordeal. 

I remember, you know, they used to have those parent-teacher conferences in the cafeteria or the gym? Where all the teachers sit at those little folding tables and the parents have to wait in line? My parents absolutely dreaded those nights. Because every single year, it was the exact same conversation. The teachers were already telling my parents back then that I just absolutely could not stay in my seat. Like, I remember my third-grade teacher actually put a square of masking tape on the floor around my desk and told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the box, because I was always wandering over to the pencil sharpener or going to look out the window at the groundskeeper mowing the grass. 

And the talking? Forget about it. I was constantly talking out of turn. I'd be blurting out answers, interrupting the teacher, interrupting the other kids when they were trying to read. I just couldn't hold a thought in my head without saying it out loud right that second. 

And that disorganized stuff we were just talking about with my truck and my desk? That started way back then, too. I lost my homework all the time. I mean, my Ninja Turtles backpack was like a black hole of crumpled up worksheets and crushed up graham crackers. I'd actually do the math sheet at the kitchen table, shove it in my bag, and then the next morning the teacher would ask for it and it was just... gone. Disappeared into thin air. 

And whenever we had an assignment or a quiz or whatever, I’d just rush right through the directions before I even really understood what they were asking me to do. Like, they’d hand out a packet and say, "Okay class, read the instructions at the top carefully," and I’d just grab my pencil and start filling in blanks or circling things, just trying to get it done as fast as humanly possible so I could go out to recess. And then I'd get the whole thing marked wrong in red ink because I was supposed to be subtracting instead of adding, or whatever it was, all because I didn't actually read what I was supposed to do. So, yeah... this isn't just a stressful job thing. It’s been exactly like this my whole life, honestly.
Do you often make careless mistakes or overlook details in your work or daily activities?

Careless mistakes? Overlooking details? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, in my line of work, if you overlook a detail, somebody could get seriously hurt, or you could end up pouring ten thousand dollars of concrete in the wrong place. So, no, I don't really do that. 

I mean, sure, like I said, my truck is a mess, and my desk is a disaster, and I'm always running behind on the paperwork, but the actual work? The construction part of it? No, I'm pretty dialed in on that. You have to be. Like, when we're framing out a commercial space, you can't just miss a detail on the blueprints. If the plans call for a load-bearing steel I-beam, you can't just throw up a couple of 2x4s and call it a day. You have to read the plans, you have to know what's going on, and you have to make sure the guys are doing it right. 

And like I said earlier about the concrete pour, I caught that the slump was off before it ever went into the forms. If I was the kind of guy who overlooked details, I might have just let them pour it, and then we'd be paying a crew to jackhammer it all out a week later. But I caught it. I saw it coming down the chute, and I knew right away it was soup. So, I don't think I make careless mistakes like that. 

I mean, yeah, I might misplace my tape measure for the fifth time in a week, or I might forget to write down a phone number, but when it comes to the actual job, the things that really matter? No, I'm on top of that. I have to be. If I wasn't, I wouldn't have lasted twenty years in this business. You just can't survive in construction if you're careless. It's too unforgiving. So, no, I really don't think I struggle with that part of things. I might be chaotic, and I might bounce around a lot, but I get the important stuff right.
Have your wife or others close to you mentioned that your behavior or symptoms are causing problems in your relationships with them?

My wife? Yeah... yeah, she has. It’s actually gotten to a really bad place with us lately. Honestly, she is just completely worn down. And I get it, I really do, because it’s got to be exhausting for her. It’s always the exact same fight. I’ll tell her, "Hey, don't worry about calling the guy to fix the garage door, I'll handle it today." And I mean it when I say it! But then I get to the site, a million things happen, and it completely evaporates from my brain. Or I'll say I'm going to pay the water bill, and I just forget until we get a shut-off notice. 

She's just so incredibly tired of having to remind me about every single little thing I said I would handle. She tells me she feels like she has three kids instead of two, because she’s constantly having to manage me and my responsibilities on top of everything else. And I hate that. I hate making her feel like my mother instead of my wife, but no matter how hard I try to keep it all straight, I just drop the ball. It really takes a toll on a marriage, you know? Just that constant disappointment.

And, you know, it's not even just at home anymore, which is what really pushed me to finally come talk to you. It's bleeding into my job in a big way. I know I was just saying how I don't mess up the actual physical construction details, like the concrete or the structural stuff, but the management side of it? It’s gotten so bad that my employer actually had to step in. 

Because, like I said, I bounce around from fire to fire so much, I end up missing these really crucial follow-ups with the architects or the vendors. And my site coordination has just been so poorly organized lately. Like, I’ll have the drywall guys show up on the exact same day the electricians are still trying to pull wire, and they can't work around each other, so it’s just a massive bottleneck and everyone's screaming at me. So, recently, the big boss actually drove down to my job trailer, shut the door, and gave me a formal concern. A documented write-up. He sat me down and said my missed follow-ups and the chaotic coordination are severely impacting the schedule, and if I don't figure out a way to get my head on straight, my job is going to be on the line. 

Twenty years in the dirt, doc, and I'm sitting there getting a formal warning like some green kid fresh out of high school. It was humiliating. So, yeah... it's causing huge problems. I just feel like I'm letting everybody down everywhere I go right now, at work and at home.
Have you ever lost a job or had significant problems at work because of your difficulties with focus, impulsivity, or organization?

Well, yeah, that’s exactly what I was just getting at a second ago. I mean, I haven't actually been fired yet, thank God, but I am absolutely on the chopping block. That formal concern I just told you about? That write-up from the big boss? That's exactly what that is. It’s because my site coordination has just been so poorly organized lately, and I'm missing all these crucial follow-ups. 

Like, I’ll get an email about a change order from the architect, and I’ll think, "Okay, I need to call the mechanical contractor right now," but then a guy walks into the trailer needing a signature for a lumber delivery, or a driver needs me to point out where to dump a load of gravel, and boom, the architect’s email is completely gone from my brain for three days. And then the trades show up to work, and they can't, because I didn't coordinate the schedule and now everybody is tripping over each other. It costs time, it costs money, and it makes the company look bad. So yeah, it's gotten bad enough at work that my employer had to officially step in and put it on paper. Sitting in that trailer, looking at a piece of paper with my name on it saying "formal concern"... man, it makes your stomach drop. 

And honestly, like I was saying, it’s the exact same dynamic at home, which is why my wife is just... she's so worn down. I know you were asking about the job, but it really is all connected. It's the exact same problem just in a different building. She is just completely exhausted from having to remind me about every single thing I said I would handle. The garage door, the bills, the gutters, whatever it is. I say I'll do it, I fully intend to do it, and then my brain just scatters to the wind the second I walk out the door. 

I'm a forty-year-old man, doc. I shouldn't need my wife to act like my personal secretary just to keep the lights on at the house, and I definitely shouldn't be getting written up like some green rookie who doesn't know how to run a job site. But that's exactly what's happening. The disorganization is just... it's catching up with me everywhere.
Have your symptoms caused problems in your relationships with friends or other family members?

Well, yeah, friends and family... it's kind of the same story there, too, honestly. I mean, I know I sound like a broken record here, talking about the work thing and my wife, but it really just bleeds into every single relationship I have. Like, just last month, my buddy Dave—we’ve been friends since high school, right?—he asked me to help him frame out a new deck on his house. And I told him, "Absolutely, man, I'm there." I even told him I'd bring my good chop saw over. 

Well, Saturday morning rolls around, and I completely forgot. I was out in the garage, trying to reorganize my toolboxes because I couldn't find a specific socket wrench, and the next thing I know, it's 2:00 PM, and my phone is blowing up with texts from Dave asking where the hell I am. And by the time I got over there, he was just... you could tell he was just so frustrated. He didn't even want my help at that point. And it's not just Dave. It's my brother, it's my parents... I'll say I'm going to show up for a family barbecue, and then I'll get completely sidetracked fixing a leaky faucet at my house, and I show up three hours late when everybody is already eating dessert. 

They don't say it to my face all the time, but I can see it in their eyes. It's that same look my wife gives me, you know? That look of, "Oh, here we go again, he dropped the ball." And it just... it eats at me. Because I'm a good guy, doc. I want to be there for my friends. I want to be the guy they can rely on. But it's like my brain just won't let me. 

And, you know, I know I already brought this up, but it really all ties back to the same exact issue I’m having at work with the site coordination and the missed follow-ups that got me that formal write-up. It's the same exact thing that has my wife so completely worn down from constantly having to remind me about every little thing I promised I'd do around the house. It's just... it's everywhere. I'm disorganized at work, I'm disorganized at home, and I'm disorganized with my friends and family. It's like I'm just constantly putting out fires and letting people down in every single area of my life, and I just don't know how to stop it. I really don't.
Are there any specific situations or activities where you feel your symptoms are most disruptive or problematic?

Specific situations? Honestly, doc, I wish I could give you a neat little answer like, "Oh, it only happens when I'm doing paperwork," or "It's only when I have to sit still in a long meeting." But... no. Not really. I mean, I've been sitting here racking my brain for months before I even made this appointment, trying to figure out if there's a pattern. Like, I'd ask myself, maybe it's just when I'm tired? Or maybe it's just when I'm stressed out with a massive concrete pour at work? But the honest truth is, there isn't one specific trigger or one specific activity. It is literally every minute of every single day. 

From the second my alarm goes off and I try to remember to start the coffee maker, to the second my head hits the pillow and I realize I completely forgot to lock the front door or take the trash to the curb. It’s like I was just saying about the job trailer, and my wife, and my buddy Dave... it doesn't matter if I'm in a high-stakes situation with the big boss breathing down my neck about a million-dollar schedule, or if I'm just supposed to be having a relaxed, easy Saturday in my own backyard. The disruption is just a constant baseline. It's everywhere. I never get a break from it. 

If I had to pick one thing, I guess I’d just have to say "life." Life is the specific situation where it's most problematic. Because whether I'm holding a rolled-up set of blueprints, or a final notice water bill, or a chop saw, my brain does the exact same thing—it just dumps whatever I'm supposed to be focusing on and completely scatters the second something else catches my eye. So, yeah, I don't think there's any one particular activity that's worse than the others. The chaos just follows me into whatever room or whatever situation I walk into, no matter how hard I try to keep it out.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, in the past?

No, doc, never. Not once. I mean, growing up back in the eighties and nineties, they didn't really look for that kind of thing unless you were a kid literally bouncing off the walls and throwing desks across the classroom, you know? I was just the kid who always lost his homework, or I’d be staring out the window during math class, completely lost in my own world. My teachers and my parents, they just thought I was lazy. That was the phrase they always used on my report cards—"He’s smart, but he’s just not applying himself." 

I barely scraped by to get my high school diploma, honestly. It was by the skin of my teeth. And after that, I figured out pretty quick that if I just went into the trades and worked with my hands, I wouldn't have to sit at a desk and read textbooks all day, which was basically torture for me anyway. So I just pushed through. I framed houses, I poured concrete, I just kept my body moving. And for a long time, the physical work kind of masked whatever this is, I guess? Because I was always on the go, always moving to the next task. 

But now that I'm a manager... now that I'm forty years old and I'm the guy sitting in the job trailer who's supposed to be running the whole show and coordinating a dozen different sub-contractors... well, like I told you, it's all just falling apart. The write-up from the big boss, my wife being so totally exhausted from managing my life for me, my buddy Dave getting ticked off... it's all coming to a head now because I can't just outwork it with a hammer anymore. 

So, no. I've never been diagnosed, never taken any medication for it, never even sat down with a doctor to talk about any of this until right now, sitting in this chair. I honestly just always thought this was a personal failing. I thought I just needed to try harder, you know? Be a better man, get a better calendar, set more alarms. My wife actually bought me three different daily planners last year. I lost two of them within a week, and the third one is currently buried under a pile of muddy invoices on the dashboard of my truck. I just never thought it was an actual medical condition I could get treated for. I just thought I was broken. But things got so bad at the site, and the tension at home got so heavy, that my wife practically begged me to make this appointment. So here I am. But yeah, no past treatment whatsoever.
Have you had any relatives, such as parents or siblings, who have been diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD?

No, not that I know of. Nobody's ever been officially diagnosed or anything like that. But, I mean, like I was just saying about how things were back when I was growing up... nobody in my family would have ever gone to a doctor for something like this anyway. 

My dad, for instance, he was a diesel mechanic, worked his absolute tail off his whole life. And looking back on it now, sitting here talking to you? Man, he was always out in the garage, always tinkering with something, could never just sit on the couch and watch a full football game with us. He’d watch maybe one quarter, and then he’d be up fixing a squeaky hinge on the screen door, and then ten minutes later he’d be out in the driveway rotating the tires on the truck. He literally could not stop moving. But if you had ever tried to tell him he had some kind of... you know, condition, or that his brain worked differently, he would have laughed you right out of the room. He just called it "having a strong work ethic" and left it at that. 

And my brother, the one I mentioned earlier who gets so fed up with me being late all the time? He's kind of cut from the exact same cloth. He’s in regional sales, always talking a mile a minute, always bouncing from one city to the next, constantly juggling a hundred different clients. Sometimes I really do wonder if he’s got a little bit of the same exact wiring that I do, you know? Because we both have that same restless energy where we just can't shut it off.
